title: Research Journal #41 — What It Would Take to Fix the Eight Failures
html:
Historical reconstruction of September 22–24, 2026

Research Journal #40 ended after four Windows rechecks brought the combined AR-1.7 audit ledger to 20 PASS, 8 FAIL and 2 INCONCLUSIVE. The next decision was to close discovery at that boundary and work out what the eight failures required of the simulation framework. A separate closure record preserved the v5 summary as it was written, including its then-open wording. AR17-016 and AR17-029 remained inconclusive. [1]

From failed cases to findings

The project reviewed the preserved observations against the frozen audit source. It recorded one finding per failing case and kept 64 supporting FAIL observations traceable to their original records. Some were repetitions or variants of the same behavior. Related findings stayed separate where the evidence pointed to different causes. The analysis used the existing run evidence and added no failure-case executions. [2]

Consider the finding on recording completion. A run could be marked complete even though the final checkpoint was missing. A checkpoint is a saved record of the run’s state that the framework can use to resume execution. That observation showed a gap in how the framework reported persistence. The audit was probing a stronger, prospective guarantee for a publication that spans several files. The finding made that qualification explicit. It also kept the possible effect on later use of the record separate from the observed gap in completion metadata. [2]

The proposed correction gave readers an explicit basis for deciding when a finished run could be treated as fully saved. Review exposed a question the proposal still had to answer. If the completion record becomes visible and the subsequent durability step fails, what should the reader report? The reviewers asked for explicit outcomes for that case and others, including missing required files and platform limits. A system could otherwise pass a test for the presence of a completion record while still giving a misleading answer to somebody using it. [3, 4]

A design review with a mixed result

The first review recorded four design-level ACCEPT decisions and four REVISE decisions. The four ACCEPT decisions meant those designs were sufficiently defined for later work. The failures still required implementation and verification of the corrections. The accepted designs addressed a bounded verification scope, ownership of release policy, validation at run entry, and all-or-nothing transfer of a batch. The four revisions concerned completion and durability, checkpoint history, the scope of static policy checks, and accounting for the tests the runner actually collects and executes. The combined corrective release was NOT READY. [4]

The review also showed what was missing from the test plan. The first matrix linked all 64 observations to proposed checks, with 86 catalog IDs in all. Those links let a reviewer trace each proposed check to its evidence. Establishing that a future check can reproduce the intended condition requires more. For example, a replay needs a healthy control that succeeds first, so that rejection of the adverse case can be attributed to the condition under test. [3, 4]

The September 24 revision kept all 86 original IDs and added 12 parent scenarios. It also proposed paired checks of scientific isolation. The purpose was to compare runs before and after a future correction to see whether changes to the software infrastructure inadvertently altered supported scientific calculations or their results. At that point the revised design and matrix still awaited review, the corrective tests were PROPOSED / NOT RUN, and scientific equivalence remained unestablished. [5]

Where this checkpoint ended

The 30 case dispositions recorded what discovery had established under its criteria. The findings explained the observed mechanisms and qualified the claims the project could make about them. The review and revision defined work that a future implementation would have to satisfy. The eight failures remained open corrective obligations at this checkpoint. [1–5]

September 26 records preserve the earlier work and document additional review and archive checks performed on that later date. The evidence here is internal software verification, documentary analysis and proposed engineering design. Scientific reproduction, new numerical physics results and physical experimental evidence were outside the scope of this work. [6]

Finding a failure is only the beginning. We also need to understand what failed, define what a correction must accomplish, and establish how we will verify that correction without introducing new problems. At this checkpoint, we had made progress toward defining those requirements, but we had not yet demonstrated that they were satisfied.

Sources

  1. BTLB, AR-1.7 Discovery Summary v5, case-dispositions-v5.json, Windows return run-20260922-185231-95e556, and Discovery Closure v1. Frozen audit 51e6d4cfe1e5b906b0691df006205160a4184f5d, baseline 2e3af1d33012c15110d470f3619eafc5ecf2f982.
  2. BTLB, AR-1.7 Findings Register and Root-Cause Analysis v1 and FINDINGS-REGISTER-v1.json.
  3. BTLB, AR-1.7 Corrective Architecture Design v1, Acceptance Matrix v1, and FINDING-ID-CROSSWALK-v1.json.
  4. BTLB, AR-1.7 Corrective Architecture Design Review v1, DESIGN-DECISIONS-v1.json, and ACCEPTANCE-MATRIX-AUDIT-v1.json.
  5. BTLB, AR-1.7 Corrective Design Revision v2, Acceptance Matrix v2, and Scientific Isolation Verification Plan v1, September 24, 2026.
  6. BTLB-SIM local preservation checkpoint 2b6c1c7819b6c8d026bf471c2c491da0f626606c and native Windows archive verification addendum 455112540aaeaccbc5859327678af4efc876f688, September 26, 2026.

The supporting evidence package contains selected records and traceability information covering discovery closure, the 64 preserved failure observations, the eight findings, the corrective-design review, and the revised acceptance plan. It does not provide a complete executable reproduction, demonstrate successful corrections, or establish independent scientific reproduction.
